items.title: The clock bridge gets a reader, and states what its bound is worth
items.body:
Closes nothing on its own — this is the work `#220` asks for, and the check it asks to have made first.

## What was missing

`robot.state`, `tof.frame` and `head_imu.frame` carry `t_ns` (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`), and `media.video` publishes the `mono_ns`/`real_ns` pair read together — that is the boot epoch the issue asks for, and it landed at v24. What did not exist was anything on the receiving side: **the pair had no reader anywhere in the repo**.

## What this does

- **`proto::clock::ClockPair`** — the bridge as a type. `media.video`'s params now read their pair through `ClockPair::now()` rather than as two bare adjacent calls, which puts "these two readings belong together" in the type instead of in a comment and leaves no way for the next caller to read them a second apart. `ClockPair::wall()` is the receiving end: the addition that turns a `t_ns` into a wall-clock moment. It has **no caller in this workspace**, and the doc comment says so — the receivers that need it are the ones §11 describes, a peer that reads RTP rather than a robot daemon.
- **A clock row in the console** — telemetry now shows a `robot.state` sample's wall-clock moment and its age.
- **§11 rewritten.** It said *wanted* / *not built*, which stopped being true at v24 and was never corrected. `AGENTS.md` says the doc is the bug when it disagrees with behaviour.

## The check §11 asked for first, and what it found

`abs-capture-time` is a dead end, but the honest version is "defined and unimplemented" rather than "does not exist":

- `webrtcsink` configures TWCC and nothing else on 0.15.3; the newer `main` adds the color-space RTP header extension as well. Neither revision touches `abs-capture-time`.
- `aiortc` does not parse it. Its `RtcpSenderInfo` does carry `rtp_timestamp`, but `aio_recv.py` never reads it.
- `webrtc-stats` has no `captureTimestamp`, but it does define `estimatedPlayoutTimestamp`, a capture-time member derived from an RTCP SR, and Chromium implements it. `webrtc-extensions` (editor's draft) additionally defines `captureTimestamp` and `senderCaptureTimeOffset` on `RTCRtpContributingSource`. So the member exists on paper; nothing on the wire fills it. `webrtc-pc`'s `RTCRtpSynchronizationSource` is still an empty extension point, and a live Chromium 131 call exposes neither member on `getSynchronizationSources()` and puts no `abs-capture-time` extmap in its SDP offer.

So frames are dated from **RTCP sender reports**, whose NTP time is the realtime clock by default (`rtpmanager`'s `ntp-time-source` is `ntp`). The part the check turned up that the section did not expect: **this only works for one kind of receiver.** Dating a frame needs the report's RTP time as well as its NTP time, and only GStreamer exposes both (`sr-rtptime` beside `sr-ntptime` in `rtpsession`'s stats). A browser does expose an `rtpTimestamp` on `getSynchronizationSources()`, but `webrtc-pc` defines it as the RTP timestamp of the media *played out* at that reading — a different moment from the SR's RTP time — so it does not close the gap. `aiortc` discards the SR's RTP half outright. Both can say what the sender's clock read; neither can say which frame it was.

## The bound

The issue asks for something written down rather than inherited from the network. An earlier version of this section got the mechanism wrong, so here is what the kernel actually does.

**The REAL−MONO offset is not a drifting rate.** `CLOCK_REALTIME` and `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` are one counter read against two basetimes: the vDSO fills both clock configurations from a single `tk->tkr_mono.mult`/`shift` pair (`kernel/time/vsyscall.c`), and NTP's frequency discipline moves that shared pair. `ntp.c` never calls `tk_set_wall_to_mono`, the only writer of the offset (`kernel/time/timekeeping.c`). So the offset moves only in steps, and the one rate the discipline does introduce is shared by both clocks.

That reorders the two error terms. `MAXFREQ` — 500 ppm, the kernel's own ceiling on that shared rate (`include/linux/timex.h`) — bounds **an interval measured on this clock**, not this conversion; quoting it here was wrong. This conversion's error is the pair's read separation instead. That one is not a bound either: both calls are served by the vDSO rather than a syscall, and the separation tracks core frequency — measured here at p50 29.5 ns with the core at 3.9 GHz and 41–48 ns at 800 MHz. It has a tail as well: 0.006% of reads over 6M samples exceeded 1 µs, and a preempted read is tens of microseconds.

The term that *is* unbounded is a **step**, because `do_settimeofday64`, `__timekeeping_inject_offset` and the leap-second path all funnel into `tk_set_wall_to_mono` and move the offset by exactly the injected amount. And the step is not hypothetical here: this board has no battery-backed RTC, boots at 1970, and NTP steps the clock (`scripts/provision.sh` says so, and `pad-link-test.sh` refuses the wall clock for the same reason). A pair taken before that first step is wrong by decades while looking like an ordinary number. Whether the clock has been set is `updater`'s judgement — `updater/src/preflight.rs` owns that floor — so this points there rather than adding a second threshold to keep in step.

(The machine this was written on has no NTP daemon running, so the argument rests on the kernel source structure above rather than on a local measurement of a disciplined clock.)

## One test changed with it

The test that reads a pair back asserted `|wall(pair.mono_ns) - pair.real_ns| < 1 µs`, commented as though that measured the read separation. It does not: `wall` applies this pair's own offset to this pair's own reading, so the result is `real_ns` **exactly** and the delta is 0 whatever the two calls cost — verified over 5M synthetic pairs, worst delta 0. Any tolerance there passes for the wrong reason, and a tight one would be flaky on a loaded board. It now asserts the identity itself (`assert_eq!`), which is the thing a consumer actually leans on, and the separation is left where it belongs: stated in the doc comment as a measurement, not asserted.

## Verification

`cargo test -p duck-ipc-proto` — 54 passed; `cargo test -p mediad` — 122 passed, so the `session.rs` and console changes are covered by mediad's own suite. `cargo fmt --check` clean, `clippy -D warnings` clean across the workspace. Additive throughout, so **no `API_VERSION` bump**.

items.title: Skills can follow the live head command (manifest `command.live`)
items.body:
Fixes #387.

## What and why

While a skill runs, robotd feeds its network zeros for the head and body command blocks, whatever the caller sends. That's right for every one-shot published so far, which were trained with `zero_command_padding`. It's wrong for a **perpetual skill trained to track the head**: for example [`cetiennec/microduck-on-sourccey-dome`](https://huggingface.co/cetiennec/microduck-on-sourccey-dome), which stands the duck on a 19 cm-radius dome and tracks the 4-D head command. As a skill it can only look straight ahead, and the console's head sliders and the pad's head mode are accepted but do nothing, with no reason given.

## Design

A manifest opts in. The default is unchanged:

```json
"command": { "encoding": "constant", "idle": [0, 0, 0], "live": ["head"] }
```

- **`command.live`**: the blocks the daemon feeds from the caller instead of zeros, `head` and/or `body`. It's read by `updaterd` on fetch (`PolicyFetchResult.live`, passed on as written) and by `robotctl policy add`, which **refuses** any other entry before writing anything. Dropping an unknown entry quietly would leave a policy that asked for a command running on zeros.
- **Config:** `live = ["head"]` in the skill's `[[policy.skill]]` table (`SkillDef.live: Vec<LiveBlock>`). It's only written when non-empty.
- **IPC:** `SkillParams.live` on `robot.skills` / `robot.addSkill`. Absent keeps what the skill had, and an unknown block is refused.
- **Control loop:** the skill arm now goes through `skill_command(def, phase, caller)`. The twist is still the skill's own (`command` / `unwind`) and never the caller's. Head and body are zeros unless named in `live`, in which case the caller's smoothed block is used (the same `command` the gait would get: head EMA + chorale + idle offset; body EMA). The live block applies in both **Holding and Unwinding**. Zeroing it for the unwind would snap the head home a second before the gait steers it back to the same command.
- **Docs:** `docs/policy-manifest.md` owns the field (field table, plus a paragraph next to `command.encoding`). `docs/design/policy-channel-design.md` §10.1 gets the reasoning in one paragraph and links to the field.

## Install consequence (API 41 → 42)

- **Downgrade with a live skill configured:** an older `robotd` won't load its config. Unknown keys inside a `[[policy.skill]]` table are not pruned the way a section's unknown keys are; I checked this against the current loader, where `Params::load` fails in both strict and lax mode. Going back below v42 with such a skill configured needs `robotctl policy remove <name>` first. A robot with no `live` skill is unaffected, because the key is never written for an empty list.
- **`robot.addSkill` with `live` to an older `robotd`:** refused as an unknown field (`SkillParams` is `deny_unknown_fields`), which is the honest answer.

This is written up in the v42 entry above `API_VERSION`.

## Tests (8 new)

- `robotd/src/control.rs`:
  - `a_skill_without_live_blocks_sees_zero_head_and_body` pins today's behaviour, including that the caller's twist never reaches a skill.
  - `a_live_head_skill_sees_the_callers_head_while_holding_and_unwinding`
  - `a_live_body_skill_sees_the_callers_body_pose`
- `robotd/src/main.rs`: `a_skills_live_blocks_are_set_kept_and_checked`. `live` is set over `robot.addSkill`, kept by a later call that leaves it out (retuning a skill's hold must not put its head back on zeros), refused for `twist`, and listed by `robot.skills`.
- `robotd-params`:
  - `a_live_head_skill_survives_the_round_trip`: `set_skill` → `robotd.toml` → the daemon's loader.
  - `a_skill_table_reads_live_blocks`: an unknown block fails the parse.
  - `a_live_list_is_parsed_or_refused_never_trimmed`
- `updater`: `a_manifest_says_which_command_blocks_it_reads_live`. It's read beside the prose `command.head`; absent means empty.

## Verified

- On macOS, `cargo test --workspace --exclude nfc`: **1595 passed, 0 failed** (27 ignored).
  - `nfc`'s `nfcd` binary doesn't build on macOS on `main` either (`nfc::spi::Spidev` is Linux-only), so I excluded it. It's unrelated to this change.
- `cargo +1.94.1 check --workspace --all-targets --exclude nfc`: OK.
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: OK.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`: no findings in the touched code. With `-D warnings` on macOS, clippy still fails on existing dead code that's only used on Linux (`body_imu_mount`, `head_imu.rs` constants), unrelated to this change.

## Not verified

- **No robot:** I haven't run a `live` head skill on hardware. The policy above is trained for it in sim only.
- **Not covered here:** `duckctl`'s add-skill command over BLE and the policy-playground Space don't pass `live`. The official set's `SetPolicy` doesn't read it either, since no set entry needs it yet. I can add those if wanted.

items.title: 香橙派 Zero 3W（A733）基础运行环境适配
items.body:
> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

本工单迁移自 [Gitea DreamweaverAI/Dreamduck #1](https://git.dreamweaverai.top/DreamweaverAI/Dreamduck/issues/1)。源码与后续开发跟踪已切换到 [GitHub serendipityshe/Dreamduck](https://github.com/serendipityshe/Dreamduck)。

## 目标

基于已同步的 Microduck 0.15.1 源码，在香橙派 Zero 3W（A733）上建立可复现的编译、安装和基础运行流程，为后续飞特舵机、IMU 和摄像头适配提供基线。

## 已确认环境

- 主板：Orange Pi Zero 3W，A733，6GB RAM。
- 主板设备树 model 为 `Orange Pi Zero 3W`；compatible 已确认为 `xunlong,orangepi-zero3w`、`arm,sun60iw2p1`。
- 存储：64GB microSD。
- 系统：Armbian 26.8.1 Minimal，Debian 13（Trixie）；主板终端报告 Debian 13.6。
- 内核：6.6.98-vendor-sun60iw2；架构：`aarch64`。
- 主板已启动并可通过 SSH 登录；Windows 继续作为编辑端，Linux 环境负责构建与验证。
- 源码基线：`1fa84386f07884e27866411bc1ba166977bced95`（Microduck 0.15.1），尚未完成本机硬件适配。
- 主板已安装 `rustc 1.99.0` 与 `cargo 1.99.0`，版本输出已由主板终端确认。

## 当前问题

官方运行环境面向 Radxa / Rockchip RK3566。现有板卡设置、摄像头 overlay、RKAIQ、RKNN 和部分 GStreamer 依赖包含 Rockchip 专用假设，不能直接按原流程用于 A733。需要先验证通用 ARM64 运行能力，再逐项处理平台专用功能。

## 实施范围

1. 核对 Rust 工具链（当前贡献规范要求 1.99+）、Linux 系统库、ONNX Runtime 和 ARM64 构建条件，形成依赖清单。
2. 明确通过 Linux / WSL 交叉编译或在主板本机编译的可复现路径，先完成 `robotd` 和 `robotctl` 的基础构建。当前先验证主板本机编译路径。
3. 梳理部署脚本的平台假设，为 A733 提供明确的板卡选择与服务配置；保留原 Radxa 配置。
4. 使用 `robotd` 的 `--fake` 后端验证进程启动与本地 IPC，不连接或驱动实际舵机。首次基础验证使用 `--fake --no-policy`；ONNX Runtime 与动作模型的加载条件单独记录。
5. 记录缺少硬件时各服务的启用条件、日志检查与恢复方法，补充开发和运行说明。

## 验收标准

- [ ] 按文档可在上述系统准备构建环境，工具链和依赖版本有记录。
- [x] 成功构建 ARM64 的 `robotd` 和 `robotctl`，并在香橙派执行；构建命令与结果有记录。
- [x] `robotd --fake` 能持续运行至少 5 分钟，客户端可通过支持的状态查询命令获得本地 IPC 响应；记录实际命令、参数与输出。
- [ ] A733 部署流程不会套用 Rockchip 摄像头 overlay 或无条件安装 RKAIQ / RKNN / Rockchip MPP；平台选择和暂不支持的功能明确可见。
- [ ] 运行项目要求的格式检查及与改动相关的测试，记录尚无法执行的板卡检查和原因。
- [ ] 文档覆盖部署、启动、停止、查看日志和重启后的验证步骤；主板重启后仍可通过 SSH 管理。

## 当前进展（2026-10-03）

- Windows 工作区已创建 `codex/orangepi-a733` 分支。
- 完整提交历史、`main` 和 `codex/orangepi-a733` 已推送到 GitHub；本机 `origin` 指向 `serendipityshe/Dreamduck`，官方仓库保留为 `upstream`。

- 使用 `./target/debug/robotd --fake --no-policy --socket /tmp/dreamduck-fake.sock` 启动，并通过 `./target/debug/robotctl --robot-socket /tmp/dreamduck-fake.sock health --json` 查询成功。健康报告记录 `healthy=true`、`achieved_hz=50.022486039266056`、`ticks=25826`、`missed=0`、总线错误为 0；按 50 Hz 估算约运行 8 分 36 秒。

items.title: Simulate the beta board on microduck 0.17.4 and use its head IMU and ToF
items.body:
Closes #61

Moves the virtual Microduck back to the **beta** board (the production design) on microduck **daemon-v0.17.4**, and makes Ito read and use the beta's head IMU and ToF. Builds on #60's tooling (head-hold, ITO_PILOT_SCRIPT, by_eye.sh, grids) and replaces its zero3 revert; #60 can be closed in favour of this.

## Sim (forks under arteeh, branch `feat/beta-sim-0.17.4`)
- arteeh/microduck `175045d` = daemon-v0.17.4 (d7560ef) + earlier sim head-IMU work (beta LSM6DSV16X served by robotd from the body at 60 Hz, zero3 BMI088 via tofd) + mediad publishing a twin's `[media.intrinsics]` like a calibrated robot.
- arteeh/microduck_rl `b06e11be` = develop b02fdea + sim head IMU / VL53L8CX ToF (0.12–3.5 m, 45°, datasheet noise) + the camera rendered at each board's mount (beta upright, rotate 0).
- `sim.py` defaults to `--board beta`: GC2093 at 720p30 (mediad's default rung), robotd `[head_imu]` on, `tofd --sim` launched (both boards), IMU/ToF datasheet noise on, head servos given upstream's ±1° gear play (add_backlash.py's model) so the camera/IMU ride off the kinematics like a real head. `--board zero3` still works.
- **GC2093 FOV is an estimate**: upstream 0.17.4 still ships no `hfov_deg` or family solve for it. The sim uses 69.7° across (1/2.9" sensor behind a 4 mm M12 lens, documented in `lens.py`, `--beta-hfov` to change) and publishes it as the robot's own `[media.intrinsics]`, the only way a real beta publishes geometry. Replace with a real beta calibration.
- The driver no longer substitutes a lens for sim frames; a robot with no published geometry (an uncalibrated beta) is refused with how to calibrate it.
- Fixed: the beta twin's frames were 2/3 gated as "blurred" because the exposure was unknown; the sim now states its instantaneous exposure.

## Ito
- Wire **v4**: `Sensors` message (camera-mounted IMU samples and multizone range grids, source-timed, mounts from robotd's head kinematics). Main builds (v3) cannot connect to this driver.
- Driver streams `head_imu.stream` / `tof.stream` when the robot serves them and carries on without either (logged, telemetry).
- Robot-first tracking: ToF zones on flat patches give metres per MASt3R unit for every frame they hit (weighted with the floor estimate); the head IMU adds gyro turn factors between consecutive nodes and the chip's gravity per node in the pose graph, and drives the blur gate. No sensors: unchanged.

## Tested by running the build (ceres, beta sim install `~/.local/share/ito-microduck-beta`)
Grids in `C:\Users\me\Projects\ito\out\by-eye\beta-board-grids\`. Two rounds main vs branch on the beta sim (room-tour route): camera upright, scale matches the camera (pilot view cropped to the camera's field), head holds still while idle and stopped. Branch reads LSM6DSV16X at 60 Hz and VL53L8CX at 15 Hz, ~90% of tracked frames ToF-scaled, 97–100% matched. **By eye the branch is the same as main**, not visibly better: a torn/doubled sofa at 47 s on main in round 1 did not repeat in round 2. Zero3 run (no head IMU, VL53L5CX) also same as main.

Untested: headset, real beta hardware, real GC2093 lens.

items.title: Overhaul 6/9: Persistent, causal Gaussian map in the live pipeline
items.body:
**Goal:** turn the #40 mapper and #41 estimator into the real live pipeline: a persistent, causal, optimized Gaussian map that keeps getting better and never jumps.

Source: [big-picture review](https://github.com/arteeh/ito/blob/316a556/docs/big-picture.md), §4 proposal 1 ("Map", "Publication", "Scheduling"), §4 "The experience all three must deliver", §6 step 5. Depends on #39, #40, #41, #42.

### Where the inputs stand (Oct 16)
- #39 is in main. #40, #41 and #42 are open and unmerged; their branches predate the PR #68 purge (24 commits behind main) and are reference, not a base:
  - `feat/gsplat-oracle` (#40): sharp with true poses, but too slow for the pilot as built (missed 90 Hz frames, floaters, failed with its own poses).
  - `feat/estimator-41` (#41): much better rotation, translation worse; DPVO retry failed. On hold.
  - `feat/obs-42` (#42): beta-sim head IMU/ToF observations; no visible gain yet.
- Start from current main (beta board only; the sim has the beta's head IMU and ToF). Port what earns its place; don't merge the old branches wholesale.

### Work
- Bounded local training on keyframes with retained observations and support/uncertainty per surface; stable surfaces accumulate evidence, recent ones are provisional and get priority.
- Map lifetime independent of estimator window: consolidate into persistent submap anchors before a keyframe is forgotten; prune by support/contribution/cost first (splats that add nothing to the view go, however new); only when the budget (Max splats or free VRAM) is full and nothing else can go, retire the least recently seen.
- Coherent publication: scene revisions carry coordinate frame, anchor transforms, observation age and a completion fence; the renderer shows the latest complete revision; superseded results can't overwrite newer ones; large corrections trigger local refit rather than visible jumps.
- One Gaussian representation with different lifetime policies (no second mesh system). Carving/replacement of the current `rgbd.py` point map retired; the new map takes over the live VRAM budget and keeps Max splats as the user's setting (default 1M, -/+ in steps of 100,000).
- The new map keeps the Precision and Input % settings working; it follows the Precision setting (Full/Half); when it runs out of GPU memory it drops the frame and shows the "reconstruction is degraded" warning, never a silent switch to Full.
- Throughout: no new missed 90 Hz headset frames and GPU memory inside the live VRAM manager.

### Done when
- The first bookshelf stays sharp after its keyframe retires; revisiting it doesn't double it; no correction moves a stationary pilot's world.
- Session recordings show it plainly better than main on the same script and Settings (textured regions sharper, no lost coverage), and new surfaces appear no later than on main.
- No new stalls or hitches in the window (headset frame timing is checked by the owner, #46); memory steady over a 10-minute session; every visible change carries the right observation age.

### How to test (see AGENTS.md)
No automated tests and no numeric gates (no dB/PSNR/LPIPS/coverage thresholds). On ceres: build the branch with `release.ps1 -Branch <branch>` and a fresh main build, record each with `uv run tools/session.py <build> <name>` against the virtual Microduck (beta board; `tools/scripts/room-tour.json`, or a longer script added to `tools/scripts/`), same Settings (Precision, Input %, Max splats) for both, and note those Settings with the result. Then look at matching frames of both runs' `screen.mp4`/`camera.mp4` with `uv run tools/frame.py VIDEO FRAME -n N` (frame numbers per step in `steps.txt`). Judge by eye; a trade-off is not an improvement. Delete recordings once judged (50 GB per job at most).

items.title: Add move-away behavior demo (CPU MuJoCo, stock walking policy)
items.body:
## Problem / use case

A common request for a small robot sharing floor space with people: when
someone walks towards it, get out of the way — but keep watching them, so the
robot can react if they change direction and so a human observer can tell the
robot has noticed them.

This PR adds that as a **CPU MuJoCo behavior demo**, not as production robot
autonomy. It shows how far a stock exported walking policy can be pushed with a
scripted supervisor, and it doubles as a rehearsal harness for the
velocity-command interface the runtime drives, in the spirit of
`scripts/infer_policy.py`.

**No new policy is trained, and no policy file is committed** — `--policy` is a
required argument.

## Implementation

Self-contained under `scripts/behavior_demos/move_away/`:

| file | role |
| --- | --- |
| `controller.py` | state machine + velocity-command law. Pure Python (no MuJoCo/ONNX/numpy) so it is fully unit-testable |
| `gaze.py` | camera-frame maths and the head visual servo |
| `perception.py` | field-of-view test + ray-cast occlusion check |
| `runtime.py` | scene path, default pose, observation layout, safe sensor lookup |
| `run_demo.py` | CLI entry point, simulation loop, optional rendering |
| `README.md` | measured constants, limitations, usage |

The behavior is `IDLE → RETREAT → TURN → CLEAR → DONE`. Heading is held
closed-loop in every walking state; the absolute trunk heading is measured each
tick and never integrated.

Also adds `src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/scene_move_away.xml`: `scene.xml`
plus a scripted **mocap** "person" prop. It is a mocap body with
`contype/conaffinity="0"`, so it adds **no degrees of freedom** (`nq` stays 21,
the keyframes stay valid) and it can never push the robot over. It follows the
existing `scene_ball.xml` pattern, so the `robot_allcollisions.xml` include
resolves the same way as the other scenes.

The observation is assembled as
`[base_ang_vel(3), projected_gravity(3), joint_pos(14), joint_vel(14), last_action(14), command(13)]`
= 61D. The demo writes only the `twist` slot and **zero-pads** `head_pose(4)` and
`body_pose(6)` rather than dropping them, per the shared-layout convention in
`AGENTS.md`.

`pyproject.toml` is unchanged. The headless path needs only `mujoco`,
`numpy` and `onnxruntime`, all already dependencies; `imageio`/`Pillow` are
imported lazily inside the rendering helper, so `--render-dir` is the only path
that needs them.

### One finding worth flagging

An earlier iteration of this demo looked up a gyro sensor named `imu_gyro`,
which **does not exist** in these models. `mujoco.mj_name2id` returns `-1` for an
unknown name, and `model.sensor_adr[-1]` is a *valid* index — the last sensor. So
the lookup did not raise: it silently fed `root_angmom` (subtree angular
momentum, kg·m²/s) into the slot the policy expects to hold rad/s.

The robot still walked and the rendered result looked plausible, which is what
makes this failure mode nasty. But every gait constant tuned against it described
the corrupted observation rather than the robot — including a "the `wz` sign is
inverted" conclusion that is simply not true with a real gyro.

Everything in this PR was re-measured against `imu_ang_vel`, and the constants
changed materially as a result:

| | against the bad observation | re-measured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| retreat speed | `vx = -0.28` | `vx = -0.36` (gait does not engage above ≈ −0.30) |
| `wz` sign | reported inverted | **normal**, with real closed-loop authority |
| turn | open-loop, cut early at 45° | closed-loop, tracked to a 15° tolerance |

`runtime.sensor_address()` now raises on an unknown sensor name, and a
regression test pins it.

## Validation

Measured with a stock exported walking policy, defaults, 22 s:

| metric | value |
| --- | --- |
| final state | `DONE`, upright |
| person visible | **1100 / 1100** control steps (`lost_steps = 0`) |
| max off-axis angle | **2.3°** from camera centre |
| heading change | **+82.8°** (90° commanded) |
| trunk height | **z = 0.116** (nominal), min 0.114 |

Robustness spot-checks: `--turn-sign -1` mirrors the maneuver (−96.5°, still
1100/1100 visible); `--person-speed 0.20` keeps 1100/1100; `--seconds 28` stays
upright at 1400/1400. Rendered frames were inspected visually — the
picture-in-picture head-camera view keeps the person centred through the turn.

## Limitations — explicitly not claimed

- **The "person" is scripted, not perceived.** A mocap prop on a fixed straight
  path, its position read from simulator state. No detector, no tracker, no real
  sensing; the visibility test is purely geometric.
- **Gaze is kinematic only.** Head pose is applied in an isolated `MjData` copy
  used solely for perception and rendering, and is never fed back into the
  locomotion dynamics. The head is a large fraction of body mass and this policy
  was never trained to compensate an externally imposed head trajectory — driving
  it physically makes the robot fall. **This PR makes no claim of physical
  head-control stability while walking**, and the numbers above do not support
  one.
- **Sim only, CPU only.** Nothing here has been validated on hardware.
- Constants were measured against one exported walking policy in this scene;
  another policy would need its own sweep.
- The head-camera optical-frame correction (the MJCF exports a quaternion whose
  optical `-Z` points backwards into the robot's own CAD) is applied to the
  **in-memory** `MjModel` only. The committed MJCF is untouched — worth a
  maintainer opinion on whether the exported camera quaternion should be fixed
  upstream instead.

## Test plan

`tests/test_move_away_demo.py` — 25 tests, all CPU, **no policy file, no GPU and
no rendering context required**:

- **State machine**: IDLE holds until the person is both close *and* visible
  (range alone must not trigger); full `IDLE→RETREAT→TURN→CLEAR→DONE` ordering;
  IDLE/DONE command exactly zero velocity; retreat speed stays inside the
  measured engagement band; heading-hold sign opposes drift correctly; `wz`
  clamping; `turn_sign` direction; the `TURN_MAX` safety timeout; command
  low-pass filtering; angle wrapping.
- **Gaze maths**: MuJoCo optical-frame convention and handedness; bearing sign;
  elevation sign; frustum rejection behind and off-axis; servo error reduction;
  the head-pitch sign convention; joint-limit margins.
- **Observation contract**: exact 61D layout with the command block zero-padded.
- **Model invariants** (compile the MJCF only): the scene path resolves; 14
  actuators and `nq == 21` (the prop adds no DoF); the person is a
  non-colliding mocap body; the gyro sensor name resolves and is not the
  `sensor_adr[-1]` fallback, and a bad name raises; the optical correction
  aligns the camera with the trunk forward axis; robot and person body subtrees
  are disjoint; `DEFAULT_POSE` matches the scene's `STAND` keyframe.

```
$ python -m pytest tests/test_move_away_demo.py -q
25 passed

$ python -m pytest tests/ -q
179 passed, 1 skipped
```

`ruff check` is clean on the added files. (`ruff format` was deliberately not
run — the existing tree does not conform to its defaults, so applying it here
would produce unrelated churn.)

## Not included

No ONNX policy, no video and no GIF are committed — only text files.

## Demo video

Fresh render from commit `39506fff` after the `imu_ang_vel` sensor fix and controller re-measurement (22 s, 1,100 frames at 50 fps, 960×640). This is not the earlier render made with the invalid sensor lookup.

items.title: Everything WebRTC carries should be timestamped at source
items.body:
Nothing this transport carries is timestamped at source. A frame arrives when it arrives, a `robot.state` notification arrives when it arrives, and a consumer that wants to know *when* the robot saw or felt something has only its own clock — which, over a relay, measures the network rather than the robot.

That is fine for driving a robot you are watching, and wrong for most of what a remote consumer is interesting for. **SLAM is the case that makes it concrete**: monocular SLAM on a stream with no capture times runs; the moment somebody wants visual-inertial — the IMU this robot has, at 50 Hz, on the same control channel — the two series cannot be related except by guessing.

Design note: [`remote-webrtc.md` §11](docs/design/remote-webrtc.md).

## Two halves, and they are not the same problem

**Media.** RTP timestamps are relative to a random offset: they order frames and date none of them. The mechanism is the `abs-capture-time` RTP header extension, which carries a wall-clock capture time per packet. **First job is checking what actually surfaces it** — whether `webrtcsink` will negotiate it, and what a browser (`RTCRtpReceiver.getSynchronizationSources`, `getStats`) and `aiortc` expose of it. A header extension nothing on the receiving side surfaces buys nothing, and that determines whether this half is cheap or a fork of somebody's stack.

**The control channel.** Ours, and cheap: a monotonic reading plus the boot epoch that makes it comparable across processes, on every notification that describes a moment (`robot.state` first). The cost is a field per message and an argument about which clock — and the answer has to be the same clock the media path ends up dating frames with, or the two series still cannot be joined.

## Why it is its own change

It alters what every notification looks like, so it wants its own `API_VERSION` bump and its own decision rather than riding along with a transport. Deliberately kept out of the remote-access slices (#209, #219).

## Done looks like

- A consumer can take a decoded frame and a `robot.state` sample and say, with a bounded error it can state, which happened first.
- The error is bounded by something written down, not by the network.

items.title: Simulate the beta board and use its head IMU and ToF in Ito
items.body:
The virtual Microduck should be the **beta** board (Seeed RK3566, the production design), not the zero3 Radxa dev kit, and Ito should work well against it, using the beta's head IMU and ToF.

PR #60 put the sim back on upstream daemon-v0.17.2 with zero3 as the default; that was the wrong direction (beta is closer to the real Microduck).

Scope:
- Sim based on microduck tag `daemon-v0.17.4` (d7560ef) plus the simulated sensors, in arteeh forks (`feat/beta-sim-0.17.4` in arteeh/microduck and arteeh/microduck_rl): GC2093 upright (rotate 0) at mediad's 720p30 rung, LSM6DSV16X head IMU read by robotd at 60 Hz, VL53L8CX ToF via `tofd --sim`, datasheet noise.
- GC2093 field of view: upstream 0.17.4 still has none (no `hfov_deg`, no family solve). The sim uses a documented estimate (69.7° across, 1/2.9" sensor behind a 4 mm M12 lens) and publishes it as the robot's own `[media.intrinsics]`, the only way a real beta publishes geometry. Must be replaced by a real beta calibration.
- Ito: Sensors message on the wire (v4), driver reads head IMU + ToF when present; robot-first tracking uses the ToF for metric scale and the head IMU's gyro/gravity as fusion factors and for the blur gate. Sensor-free path unchanged.
- Keep PR #60's tooling (head-hold vs robotd idle_head, ITO_PILOT_SCRIPT, by_eye.sh, grids).
- Judged by running the build with `e2e/by_eye.sh` against the beta sim, versus main, by eye.

items.title: Merge the beta board work and purge tests, docs and comments; beta Microduck only
items.body:
Closes #65
Closes #59
Closes #61
Closes #63
Closes #66

Built on `feat/beta-board`, which already includes PRs #60, #62 and #64. GitHub will mark those PRs merged when this one is merged.

**What's in it**
- **Merged work:** the beta board sim and Ito's use of its head IMU and ToF (#61); the head-hold fix (#59); frames rendered at exact sim time, which reduces horizon wobble (#63). The wobble fix is kept.
- **Gaze commands (#66):** `robotd` sent `robot.look` absolute joint angles, but the policy expects angles relative to its home pose (neck and head pitched up 20°). The microduck fork (`03e3fd0`, branch `feat/beta-sim-0.17.4`) now converts them. Holding a look to the side no longer rolls the camera. A small slow drift while standing still remains: the robot itself settling after resume. The real robot needs the new daemon.
- **Tests:** `e2e/` is gone, about 15,000 lines. Two tools replace it:
  - `tools/session.py BUILD NAME` starts the virtual Microduck and a Windows build of Ito, then runs a pilot script from `tools/scripts/` (keys, head turns and tilts, commands, key presses, clicks on overlay controls). It writes `screen.mp4` (the Ito window, overlay included), `camera.mp4` (the robot camera frames Ito received), `steps.txt` (when each script step starts in the video), `ito.log` and the sim logs.
  - `tools/frame.py VIDEO FRAME [-n COUNT]` saves one frame, or several consecutive frames side by side (frame numbers, so neighbouring frames can be compared), using the ffmpeg bundled with `imageio-ffmpeg` (dev group).
  - Test-only hooks are removed (sim truth poses, SLAM oracle poses). `ITO_RECORD` now records the whole window, overlay included.
- **Docs:** `VISION.md`, `docs/measure*`, `docs/gpu-budget*` and `docs/motion-sheets.md` are deleted. `docs/big-picture.md` stays. `AGENTS.md` is 21 lines: a pointer to the README intro, a map of the code, and how to work. The README's e2e sections are replaced by a short testing paragraph.
- **Comments:** 180 of 914 comments and docstrings are kept. They cover units, axes and frames, platform and library quirks, and safety invariants. The long ones are shortened.
- **Beta only:** the zero3 code is gone from Ito's side: lens, camera mount and rotation, the BMI088 noise entry, and the sim's `--board` option. The Pollen forks under `third_party/` still contain our zero3 tofd head-IMU simulation (`arteeh/microduck` 721aa4b). Removing it is a follow-up because it needs a sim rebuild.

Python is down from about 31,300 lines to 16,200.

**Tested:** I built `builds\feat-merge-purge` and recorded the room-tour script against the beta sim (`out\sessions\purge-2`). It connected, reconstructed, ran all 26 steps, and wrote both videos and the step times. The camera is upright. Not tested on a headset or real hardware.

**After merging:** the shared sim install (`~/.local/share/ito-microduck`) is still the old v3 / zero3-era build, and main's builds won't connect to it. Re-run `drivers/microduck/setup-sim.sh` from main. The separate beta install `~/.local/share/ito-microduck-beta` can go after that.

items.title: Pilot regressions: head hold, scripted by-eye sessions, sim back on main
items.body:
Closes #59

- **Sim back on main.** setup-sim.sh was re-run from main on ceres: microduck 35b71a2 (daemon-v0.17.2) and microduck_rl b02fdea. The `microduck-sim` launcher points at ~/Projects/ito/main again. No code change.
- **Head hold** (drivers/microduck/adapter.py). robotd 0.17 starts an idle look-around 2 s after the last head intent. Ito sent looks only while the pilot held the deadman. The driver now re-sends the last aim (with roll) every 0.5 s when no look has gone out. Before the first look it sends straight ahead.
- **Scripted pilot** (ito/desktop/input.py). This is opt-in: `ITO_PILOT_SCRIPT=route.json` drives the desktop pilot (WASD keys, head turn/tilt rates, resume/stop/recenter) whatever window has focus.
- **e2e/by_eye.sh BUILD NAME**: runs the sim, opens the Windows build with ITO_RECORD and the route, and makes motion sheets. **e2e/camera_grid.py** and **e2e/view_grid.py** put runs side by side. The route is e2e/routes/room-tour.json (2.5 min).
- **AGENTS.md**: the test is running the build; never change the shared sim install from a branch.

Results by eye (C:\Users\me\Projects\ito\out\by-eye on ceres):
- On main's sim, neither this build nor feat/recon-40-41 shows the wrong scale (compare-main-vs-recon.jpg). recon-40-41 ghosts more than main: doubled table legs, smeared sofa.
- The head stays put through every hold, both with and without the hold (head-hold-*.jpg). robotd 0.17.2's idle look-around did not trigger in these sessions, so the hold is a guard and is unproven against the newer robotd that moved the head.
- A 720p sim camera is no sharper than 360p (compare-360p-vs-720p.jpg). The blur comes from fusion, not input resolution, and is #43's work.

Not tested: the headset, the real robot.

items.title: v8 velstand: inconsistent pure lateral starts and yaw drift in MuJoCo/Warp CPU
items.body:
# v8 velstand: inconsistent pure lateral starts and yaw drift in MuJoCo/Warp CPU

Hi, I am investigating inconsistent pure lateral motion with the released v8 `velstand.onnx` policy. This may be related to #59, although that report and its simulator results mainly concern v5.

I am reporting observations and asking for configuration guidance. I have not established a source-code defect or tested this on a physical robot.

## Environment

- Policy: `pollen-robotics/microduck-policies`, revision `v8`, `velstand.onnx`.
- Policy SHA256: `2fc7f8ee6acd7d0d3f66a99927b5d5a56589aeed02ec714de329b252d5ccf492`.
- Local base checkout: `b26950afb74432b53fe81c4d322988a3785ea0a6`, with local diagnostic changes.
- macOS / arm64; Warp CPU, no CUDA GPU.
- MuJoCo 3.10.0, mjlab 1.3.0, warp-lang 1.12.0, Torch 2.9.1, NumPy 2.4.1, ONNX Runtime 1.24.4.
- BAM pinned to `62bd8ce12154340be97e06f7f41a0ca8f116d967`.
- Physics 200 Hz; deterministic ONNX inference 50 Hz; 61 actor observations and 14 actions. The published policy weights were unchanged.

## Diagnostic setup and limitations

**This is a locally modified diagnostic configuration derived from VelStand, not an untouched upstream task.**

It uses flat terrain and the all-collisions/backlash robot with BAM. It starts upright at root z=0.125m / yaw=0, disables prone initialization and injected pushes, and fixes head/body commands to zero. Domain randomization, actor observation corruption and IMU mounting error are disabled; BAM voltage is 7.4V with drop gain 0.1. Physics uses 5ms implicitfast, 30 solver iterations and 50 line-search iterations. Physical command/sensor delays remain enabled.

The local wrapper also changes rewards, termination settings and critic observations; no training or critic inference was performed, and no falls or environment resets occurred during this probe.

The policy was evaluated directly in the mjlab/MuJoCo Warp environment, bypassing Studio, HTTP controls and robotd. No external heading controller or added yaw command was used. These results come from **three parallel environments with one seed (0)**, not three independent seeds.

## Command sequence

Command axes are `[vx, vy, vyaw]`; head/body commands remain zero:

1. Stand: `[0, 0, 0]` for 2s.
2. Left: `[0, +0.3, 0]` for 10s.
3. Stop for 3s.
4. Right: `[0, -0.3, 0]` for 10s.
5. Stop for 3s.
6. Left again: `[0, +0.3, 0]` for 10s.

## Observed results

Displacements and yaw excursions are measured relative to the trunk heading at the beginning of each segment. Maximum yaw is the largest absolute yaw departure during the entire 10s segment.

| Environment | Initial left displacement | Right displacement | Right maximum yaw excursion | Left after right displacement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | +0.0063m | -0.5302m | 13.40° | +0.4706m |
| 1 | +0.0062m | -0.5450m | 10.26° | +0.4435m |
| 2 | +0.4657m | -0.5375m | 16.54° | +0.0066m |

Three of the nine lateral segments barely moved; the other six did move. The main observations are inconsistent initiation and yaw drift under zero commanded yaw. I am not claiming that every segment is immobile or that a local acceptance threshold is an official requirement.

## Questions

1. Is reliable pure lateral motion from rest (`vx=0, vy=±0.3, vyaw=0`) expected with the released v8 VelStand policy?
2. Are there recommended scene, BAM, voltage, action-filtering or command settings for reproducing this checkpoint's lateral behavior?
3. Could the nominal evaluation changes or Warp CPU backend explain these observations? Is there a known-good upstream reproduction command/configuration to compare against?

I would like to verify configuration compatibility before attributing this to the policy or training recipe. The numerical report can be attached as `v8-lateral-observations.json`; its pass/fail fields use local diagnostic limits, not official criteria. The existing local probe depends on local configuration modules, so it is not yet a standalone upstream reproduction script.

[v8-lateral-observations.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33923720/v8-lateral-observations.json)

items.title: Microduck: a head gyro computed through the neck, its A/B, and the head IMU on the real robot
items.body:
> **Note: Microduck work is briefly paused, pending a response from Pollen on PR-2 (pollen-robotics/microduck#381).**
> ★ MV stays the promoted stack; the port plan's resume point says what to pick up afterwards.

## What this asks

The head brain reads a head gyro that our scene adds, and our gap table said the real robot has none. Two questions: what
does the robot actually have, and could something else give the head the same behaviour?

## The hardware

The robot does have a head IMU. Upstream PR #232 (2026-09-07..10, after our 2026-09-01 audit) added `head_imu.stream`:
gyro and accelerometer, with the sensor's pose on `robot.state.frames.head_imu`. On the zero3 board it is a BMI088 served by
`tofd` and **off by default**; on the beta board it is on at 60 Hz.

## The substitute

The head's angular rate is the trunk gyro plus each neck joint's axis times its velocity, both already on `robot.state`.
`DuckBody::head_gyro_fk` computes it, and two host options use it:

- `--head-gyro-fk QUANT LAG`: the head brain gets the computed gyro, each neck velocity rounded to QUANT rad/s (the XL330's
  resolution is 0.02398) and LAG ticks old
- `--head-gyro-zero`: the head brain's gyro inputs read zero (the lesion)

With both off, the binary is tick-identical to the previous one (240 s, seed 7).

## Results (★ MV, n = 24 fixed seeds, with a placebo arm)

| arm | head pitch-axis shake | body points at the target | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| control | 0.684 rad/s | 44 % | — |
| computed, exact | identical | 44 % | TAUTOLOGY (rigid sim) |
| computed, rounded, no lag | +0.110 | 43 % | NULL (inside the placebo's range) |
| computed, rounded, 1 tick late | +0.154* | 45 % | PARTIAL; the operator watched it: "the head looks fine" |
| gyro zeroed | +0.362* | 36 % | REGRESSION, loud |
| placebo | +0.060 | 43 % | — |

\* the paired 95 % interval excludes 0.

- **The gyro is load-bearing**, and the computed one replaces it in simulation.
- **Escapes rose in both computed arms** (+1.5 and +1.9 a run, against +0.4 for the placebo). This is unexplained; a second
  placebo would settle it.
- **Unmodelled:** the neck's flex and gear backlash, which the joint encoders miss. Re-measure against the real head IMU on
  hardware before choosing between them.

Full write-up: design doc §17.119.

## Changes

- `mj_host/src/DuckBody.{hpp,cpp}`, `mj_host/src/main.cpp`: the computed gyro, the two options and their log fields
  (`hwf`, `hws`)
- `tools/duck_launcher/presets.json`: presets HG LAG (seed 4, the worst head shake) and HG CTL
- Docs: design doc §17.119; the port plan's status and resume point (the pause); dated corrections where we said the robot
  had no head IMU; the `mj_host/README.md` gap row; the playroom plan's hardware check

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: Microduck sim: main WSL distro, upstream daemon-v0.17.2 (velstand v8)
items.body:
Closes #55

The simulated Microduck now runs in the default WSL distro (Ubuntu 26.04) from `~/.local/share/ito-microduck`, built by `setup-sim.sh` from the `third_party/` pins: microduck **`daemon-v0.17.2`** (was 77005fd, 0.16.0), microduck_rl **develop b02fdea** (was 273afe0), and MuJoCo 3.10.0 from microduck_rl's `uv.lock` (was a hand-picked 3.3.7). The first commit pinned microduck's main (969057e); 81399d4 moves it to the release tag.

## What broke, and the fixes (all on Ito's side)

| Broke | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| No video: mediad ended every session | GStreamer 1.28's `rtph264pay` rejects aiortc's `42e01f` answer against x264's `42c01e` (Ubuntu 26.04) | the driver answers with the offered profile-level-id (`remote.py`) |
| Body turned ~2x too fast; 130 degree look turned 69 degrees | velstand **v8** (0.17's policies) tracks yaw; our v7 dead-zone remap overshot | send the rate itself (`yaw_command`) |
| Camera 2.4 degrees low looking 15 degrees up | v8 stands with the neck lower; tilt trim hit its 25 degree limit | limit 35 degrees |
| 60 degree look landed 51 degrees (v7: 53) | robot.look lands standing looks ~15% short | learned pan trim, standing/turning in place only |
| Viewer had no title bar (Wayland) | pyGLFW picks 26.04's GLFW 3.4, which prefers WSLg's Wayland | the wheel's X11 GLFW on WSL |
| Closing the viewer: body SIGSEGV | head-camera thread rendered after GLFW went | stop it before the viewer closes and at exit |

Also: the launcher puts this checkout ahead of the venv's copy of the driver (the sim is never stale); `setup-sim.sh` moves an existing prefix to new pins; Windows `.cmd`/`.ps1` use the default distro.

## Tests on Ceres

- Walking e2e, isolating the cause: old distro + old pins: 1 known fail (backward-stop dip); new stack + **v7** policies: 15/15; new stack + v8: 4-6 fails; with the fixes: **15/15 twice** at 0.17.2.
- `microduck_scene`, `_camera`, `_lens`, `_lifecycle`, `_link` (90 Hz poses), `microduck.py` (pilot + e-stop), `_viewer` (window, screenshot, clean close): all pass.
- Windows: `ito-microduck.cmd` starts the sim and viewer, `builds\main\ito\ito.exe` connects, re-pairs once, then reconnects as a known pilot; live video, reconstruction 5.2 frames/s.

## Not covered

- A real duck still on a v7 release would now under-turn (yaw sent unremapped).
- Headset untested. Head IMU is still unsimulated upstream.
- The old `ito-microduck` distro is untouched; removing it waits for the owner.

strands-robots v1: The design and part-by-part refactor
items.body:
> [!IMPORTANT] > **Pinned. This is the v1 contract; the dates are in the roadmap, #3818.** Every v1 pull request says `Part N of #4749` and does exactly one part from [the plan](#the-plan-part-by-part). A PR that has to leave this design writes the change here as a comment *before* making it. Decisions 15-19 were added on Oct 15; the old body is preserved in the comments. ## v1 in one sentence **A `Simulation` is a world. A `Robot` is a body in a world, or on a bus. A `Policy` turns an `Observation` into an `Action`.** Everything else (the mesh, tools, recording, the dashboard) is written once against those three and never again per backend. ```python from strands import Agent from strands_robots import Mesh, Policy, Robot, Simulation arm = Robot("so101") # joins Simulation.default() g1 = Robot("g1", position=[1, 0, 0]) # the SAME world assert arm.sim is g1.sim arm.act({"shoulder_pan": 0.3}) # one control step of world time g1.run(Policy("holosoma"), seconds=10) # observe -> policy -> act, written once arm.run(Policy("zenoh://gpu:7447/smolvla"), instruction="pick the cube", seconds=20) # any lerobot-policy-server sim = Simulation("isaac", device="cuda:0") # pick another world explicitly arm2 = Robot("so101", sim=sim) batch = Simulation(physics="newton", num_envs=1024) real = Robot("so101", port="/dev/tty.usbmodem...", confirm=operator_says_yes) real.calibrate() # LeRobot calibration JSON, unchanged real.estop() # from any thread; always wins; resume(approved_by=) releases it lab = Mesh("zenoh://", tenant="lab-a") # every robot on the LAN, zero config lab.mount(real) Agent(tools=[arm.tool, g1.tool, sim.tool, lab.tool])("look around, then wave") ``` --- ## Why Read against `main` @ `5386b9c0` (v0.5.3 + 1): - **`Robot` is not a class.** `robot.py:636` is a factory typed `-> Simulation | HardwareRobot | HardwareDriver`. In sim mode it builds a world and returns the engine, so the "robot" you hold is a `MuJoCoSimEngine` (8,125 lines, 110 methods, 9 bases) with one robot in it. - **Two robots means two worlds.** `Robot("so101")` then `Robot("g1")` gives two engines that cannot see each other; the dashboard runs a process per card stitched back over the mesh (979-line `DeviceManager`). - **Isaac makes the current model impossible.** `SimulationApp` can exist once per process; a second Isaac robot silently gets the first app. - **Newton is a solver, not a world**, yet it is a third 3,179-line `SimEngine` that copies scene loading, cameras, recording and randomization. - **Sim and hardware share no type**, so the policy runner, recorder, teleop and mesh were each written twice, and safety lives in three side modules instead of on the robot. Result: 260,105 lines in the package. The v1 reference does the whole job, safety and mesh included, in **10,459**. --- ## The design ### 1. One world `Simulation.default()` is process-global, like `asyncio.get_event_loop()`. It is created on first use: MuJoCo, headless. ### 2. Five types `Description` (what a robot is), `Simulation` (a world), `Robot` (a body in it, or on a bus), `Policy` (what it does next) and `Body`, the only thing that differs between a simulated, a real and a remote robot. ### 3. One loop `Robot.run` is written once. It checks the policy's `Requirements` and units before step one, and ends with a `RunResult` that says why it stopped: `steps`, `stop_when`, `stopped`, `fault` (the policy gave up) or `estop`. ### 4. Thirteen methods make a simulator ### 5. A real robot brings its twin ### 6. A robot is a device Every robot, sim or real, generates its own **manifest** (sensors, controls with `range`, `safe` and `on_disconnect`, rpcs, events). Every write that is not the developer's own code passes **one safety chain**: range, safe, interlocks, validators, the operator gate. `estop()` bypasses the chain, takes no lock, and latches until `resume(approved_by=)`. ### 7. Any robot, anywhere: the mesh ### 8. Any policy, any robot ### 9. The dashboard is a twin of one world ### 10. One concept, one package --- ## The interfaces The whole top level is `strands_robots.__all__`: ```python Robot, Simulation, Policy, Body, Description, Observation, Action, JointState, Pose, Mesh, __version__ ``` Everything else is imported from the package that owns it: `strands_robots.simulation`, `.robot.device`, `.robot.safety`, `.robot.drivers`, `.policy`, `.policy.lerobot`, `.mesh`, `.recording`, `.tools`, `.dashboard`, `.units`.
Simulation: one world, owns time, holds many robots ```python class Simulation: def __init__(self, backend: str = "mujoco", *, physics: str = "native", # "native" | "newton" (MuJoCo-Warp) timestep: float = 0.002, substeps: int = 10, headless: bool = True, device: str | None = None, num_envs: int = 1, # > 1 needs physics="newton" gravity=(0, 0, -9.81), ground: bool = True, render_size=(640, 480)) -> None @classmethod def default(cls) -> Simulation # the world a Robot joins when given none # time def step(self, n: int = 1) -> None def control_step(self) -> None # what one act() costs a simulated robot def manual_time(self) -> ContextManager[Simulation] def reset(self, *, keyframe: str | None = None, seed: int | None = None) -> None time: float; physics: Physics; envs: int; revision: int; lock: RLock # scene robots: Mapping[str, Robot] def add(self, robot, *, position=None, orientation=None, keyframe=None) -> Robot # Robot.__init__ calls it def remove(self, robot: Robot | str) -> None def add_object(self, name, *, shape=None, path=None, size=None, position=None, mass=None, color=None) -> Object def set_pose(self, body: Robot | Object | str, position=None, orientation=None) -> None # teleport def camera(self, name, *, position, target=None, fov=45, size=None, attach=None) -> SceneCamera def render(self, camera=None) -> np.ndarray def randomize(self, *, friction=None, mass=None, lighting=None, seed=None) -> None def contacts(self) -> list[Contact] # loop, agents, lifecycle def run(self, policies: Mapping[Robot, Policy], **run_options) -> dict[str, RunResult] # lock-step def describe(self) -> dict # robots, objects, cameras, physics, time: the dashboard reads THIS tool: AgentTool # add robot/object/camera, step, reset, render (an image back) def close(self) -> None # also a context manager ``` `Simulation("isaac")` steps PhysX under its one `SimulationApp` (a second one in the process is refused until `close()`); `physics="newton"` belongs to the MuJoCo backend. Both are imported only when such a world is made.
Backend: the only thing a new simulator implements ```python class Backend(ABC): def load(self, scene: Scene) -> None # (re)build from plain data; joint state of surviving bodies carried over def step(self, n: int) -> None def reset(self, keyframe: str | None) -> None def time(self) -> float def joint_state(self, body: str) -> JointState def set_targets(self, body: str, targets: np.ndarray) -> None def body_pose(self, body: str) -> Pose # floating bodies fill linear/angular velocity def set_pose(self, body: str, pose: Pose, *, zero_velocity: bool = True) -> None def set_gains(self, body: str, kp: np.ndarray, kd: np.ndarray) -> None # a policy's PD travels with the policy def render(self, camera: str) -> np.ndarray def contacts(self) -> list[Contact] def physics(self) -> Physics def close(self) -> None ``` Implementations live under `strands_robots/simulation/backends/{mujoco,isaac,newton}/`. mjlab is not a backend: it is `Simulation(physics="newton", num_envs=N)`.
Robot: the one type a user holds ```python class Robot: def __init__(self, name: str, *, # registry key ("so101", "g1", ...) or a path to MJCF/URDF sim: Simulation | None = None, # None -> Simulation.default(), unless port=/driver= is given port: str | None = None, driver: str | Driver | None = None, cameras: Mapping[str, int | str] | None = None, # hardware only position=None, orientation=None, keyframe: str | None = None, id: str | None = None, # unique in its world: so101, so101_2, ... twin: bool = True, # hardware: a free twin in Simulation.default() confirm: Callable[[np.ndarray], bool] | None = None, # hardware: the operator gate mesh: Mesh | None = None) # sugar for mesh.mount(robot) # the verbs def observe(self, *, images: bool = True) -> Observation def act(self, action: Action, *, steps: int | None = None) -> Observation # the developer's own call def confirm_act(self, action: Action, *, steps=None, confirmed=False) -> Observation # what tools, the mesh and # the dashboard call: through the safety chain def calibrate(self, *, interactive: bool = True) -> Calibration # the loop, written once for every body def run(self, policy, *, instruction=None, hz=None, seconds=None, steps=None, stop_when=None, units="auto", realtime=False, record=None, push=False) -> RunResult # hz: the policy's, else 30 def start(self, policy, **run_options) -> Task # background: Task.stop() / .status / .result def stop(self) -> RunResult | None # a robot is a device manifest: Manifest # generated from the Description and the body def describe(self) -> dict # the manifest as JSON + live task and estop state def estop(self) -> None # any thread, no chain, no lock; latches def resume(self, *, approved_by: str) -> None # only a named operator releases the latch def hold(self) -> None def subscribe(self, event: str, cb, *, hz=None) -> Callable[[], None] # "state": the observation's joints, t, seq estopped: bool; supports_position_hold: bool # placement (sim only; hardware raises, its twin can still be teleported) pose: Pose def set_pose(self, position=None, orientation=None) -> None def set_gains(self, kp, kd) -> None # identity and agents name: str; id: str; description: Description; sim: Simulation | None; body: Body is_real: bool; twin: Robot | None; twin_of: Robot | None; action_keys: tuple[str, ...] tool: AgentTool # generated from the manifest's rpcs def close(self) -> None ```
Data: Observation, Action, JointState, Pose, and the types that live with their owner ```python @dataclass(frozen=True) class Observation: t: float joints: JointState # names + positions / velocities / efforts (SI: rad, rad/s, N·m) pose: Pose | None # base pose in the world frame (+ twist for floating bases) images: Mapping[str, np.ndarray] # camera -> HxWx3 uint8 extras: Mapping[str, Any] # imu, contacts, battery ... per body def __getitem__(self, joint: str) -> float def to_lerobot(self) -> dict # "observation.state", "observation.images." Action = np.ndarray | Mapping[str, float] # joint targets in Description.action_keys order; validated once, in Robot.act @dataclass(frozen=True) class Pose: position; orientation # (w, x, y, z); linear_velocity, angular_velocity: optional # with their owner (decision 14) strands_robots.policy.Requirements # images {cam: (w, h)}, state_dim; checked before step one, refused by name strands_robots.robot.run.RunResult # steps, seconds, hz_target, hz_achieved, stopped_by, recorded, final, fault strands_robots.robot.drivers.Calibration # LeRobot's calibration JSON, read and written as is strands_robots.simulation.Physics, Contact, Scene, Object ```
Policy: one factory, picked by the form of the spec ```python class Policy: # Policy(spec) returns the right subclass; subclassing it is a plain constructor def act(self, obs: Observation, *, instruction: str | None = None) -> Action def reset(self) -> None def requirements(self) -> Requirements units: str | None # a unit scheme ("rad", "lerobot"), or units_for(description) for a checkpoint # optional hooks the run loop honours: attach(robot) / detach(), hz, realtime, gains = (kp, kd) Policy(lambda obs: ...) # any callable Policy("holosoma") # ONNX presets (strands_robots/policy/onnx/presets.json, data): Policy("microduck", vx=0.3) # holosoma (G1) and the ten microduck skills: Policy("microduck?skill=roulade") # alpha_walking velstand alpha_stand alpha_sitstand ball_kick_left/right from_spec("microduck?skill=velstand&wz=1") # roller roller_crouch roulade alpha_ground_pick Policy("lerobot/smolvla_base") # a LeRobot checkpoint in-process, through LeRobot's own load_deployment Policy("zenoh://gpu:7447/smolvla") # any lerobot-policy-server, through LeRobot's own client (chunks, RTC) ChunkedPolicy(inner, replan_every=None) # holds an action chunk and replays it; lives in policy/, never in the sim from strands_robots.policy.lerobot import server_config, write_server_yaml, serve server_config(robot.description, "lerobot/smolvla_base") # the server's YAML from the robot + the checkpoint ``` A LeRobot deployment's names (`.pos`), cameras and units (its `semantics` label, mapped by `units/semantics.json`) are checked against the robot **before a session exists**; a lost server, a deadline or a stale chunk raises `PolicyFault` and the run ends `stopped_by="fault"`.
Device and safety: strands_robots.robot.device, strands_robots.robot.safety ```python @dataclass(frozen=True) class Manifest: device_id: str; device_type: str; name: str; real: bool; position_hold: bool tenant: str; labels: Mapping[str, str]; twin: str | None; twin_of: str | None sensors: tuple[Sensor, ...] #
Driver: a hardware Body ```python class Driver(Protocol): names: tuple[str, ...] # the Description's action_keys, in order def read(self) -> JointState def write(self, targets: np.ndarray) -> None def pose(self) -> Pose | None def images(self) -> Mapping[str, np.ndarray] def extras(self) -> Mapping[str, Any] def hold(self) -> None # keep the current positions under torque def estop(self) -> None # the fastest stop the bus has; takes no world or run-loop lock def calibrate(self, *, interactive: bool = True) -> Calibration # LeRobot's calibration JSON, read and written as is def close(self) -> None supports_position_hold: bool # registry hardware.position_hold, else the driver's own answer ``` 1.0 drivers: `feetech` (SO-100/101: read, write, torque, calibrate; exact LeRobot `degrees` from a calibration), `unitree` (G1/Go2/H1 over DDS: observe), `microduck` (robotd: observe). The driver is registry data (`hardware.driver`).
Mesh: every device, anywhere (from strands_robots import Mesh) ```python class Mesh: def __init__(self, transports="zenoh://", *, tenant=None, presence_ttl=3.0, operator=None, resume_authority=None, resume_key=None) # "zenoh://", "iot://us-west-2", "memory://", or several def mount(self, robot, *, device_id=None, labels=None, state_hz=None, watchdog_ms=500.0) def unmount(self, device_id: str) -> None def discover(self, selector="device(*)", *, min_count=0, timeout=0.0) -> list[Device] # device(role:arm,type:robot_arm) def invoke(self, device_id: str, rpc: str, *, timeout=2.0, **args) # through ITS safety chain def subscribe(self, device_id: str, event: str, cb) -> Callable[[], None] # "state": same payload as in-process def connect(self, device_id: str, *, images=False) -> Robot # a Robot whose Body is a RemoteBody def broadcast(self, command, *, selector="device(*)", deadline=1.0, approved_by=None) -> list[str] # who acked tool: AgentTool # use_mesh, generated from the manifests present def close(self) -> None ``` Keys (zenoh): `strands///{manifest,state,event/,rpc/}` and liveliness `strands//@presence/`; scouting only on `224.0.0.224:7447`. Over AWS IoT Core rpcs are confirmed Direct Messages, so a device that is away answers 404 at once and nothing is queued. A device whose controller vanishes applies `on_disconnect`; resume is the stopping operator's (in-process / loopback) or a fresh Ed25519-signed assertion.
Recording, tools, dashboard ```python robot.run(policy, seconds=10, record="datasets/so101") # LeRobot v3 through LeRobot's own writer; robot.run(policy, seconds=10, record="hf://me/so101", push=True) # one episode per run, resumable; meta/units.json says # which units; only hf:// with push=True uploads robot.tool, sim.tool, mesh.tool # strands agent tools, generated from the manifest and # the verbs; an agent can estop, never resume or calibrate from strands_robots.dashboard import Dashboard Dashboard(sim, robots=[real], model=..., mesh=lab).serve(port=8090) # GET /api/scene, WS /ws/state, WS /ws/chat, # POST /api/robots/{id}/act (X-Confirm on a real body); # loopback only; standalone in the browser with no server ```
--- ## Decisions | # | question | decision | |---|---|---| | 1 | default world | `Simulation.default()`, process-global.
